To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we found a low dimensional representation of the motor commands for vowel production that is robust to changes in the speaker's physiology and that we were able to link this representation in terms of active and inactive points to the anatomical description of the vocal tract, and to the neuronal activations of the motor commands in the cortex, thus proposing a global strategy for vowel production.

1) the vocal tract can be described in terms of a few discrete points, 2) the dynamics of these points can be captured in a discrete low-dimensional space, 3) this space is related to the anatomy of vocal tract and 4) this space is also related to the neural activations for vowel production

the dynamics of three Hall-effect transducer signals can be used to describe vowel articulation in a discrete low-dimensional binary space, and that this representation is consistent with the anatomy of the human vocal tract, with previous reports of highly tuned neural activations for vowel production in monkeys, and with recent reports of highly selective neuronal activations in humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a low dimensional motor representation for the vocal tract, which can be related to the underlying neuronal activity and the resulting acoustic output, and which can be used for the control of a robotic voice synthesizer.
the study of motor control of the vocal tract during speech, and with the development of a discrete motor description of the speech production process.
the study of the neural control of vocalization, and in particular with the role of discrete motor coordinates for vowel production in the human vocal tract.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present work shows that the vocal production for vowels can be described in terms of a discrete low dimensional representation, and that this representation is related with the neural activity of the vocal production.
the motor control of speech is based on a small number of discrete motor commands.
the motor description of vowel production is a low dimensional space of binary patterns, and the motor control of speech is a global strategy for vocalization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found an effective and robust way for vowel classification, and a simple model for motor coordination in speech.
we have found an effective way to describe the dynamics of vowels in terms of simple motor commands that are robust to the variability of the speech production apparatus.

vowels are produced in the human by a set of motor coordinates, and that the dynamics of these coordinates are the result of a complex interaction between the peripheral dynamics and the central nervous system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human motor system for speech production is likely to be much more parsimonious than the models currently employed in speech production research.
the motor space for vowels can be reduced to a small discrete set of motor coordinates, which can be easily mapped to the anatomy of vocal production.
the motor space for vowel production is discrete and low dimensional.
